title: AXI4 QoS: Tag, Policy, and Ordering
description: Follow an illustrative default higher-value-first policy, then inspect the ordering-constrained request to see why AxQOS is an input to system arbitration rather than a protocol guarantee of immediate service.
labels: Higher-first is the specified default policy recommendation

phases.name: AR request
phases.description: The display master presents ARQOS with the read address. The tag is captured with the AR handshake.

phases.name: Chosen
phases.description: In this illustrative default policy, the higher eligible QoS value is selected before the CPU request.

phases.name: Service
phases.description: The selected transaction progresses. AXI does not define an exact latency or service deadline from the tag alone.

phases.name: AR request
phases.description: The CPU request is simultaneously eligible but carries the lower value in this configured example.

phases.name: Policy wait
phases.description: The request waits under the illustrated policy. A real implementation can use a more sophisticated compatible QoS method, including aging or bandwidth regulation.

phases.name: Service
phases.description: The CPU request progresses after the earlier selection. Verification needs the configured policy and fairness contract to judge this latency.

phases.name: AR request
phases.description: A high tag does not erase ordering relationships carried by the transaction ID and destination history.

phases.name: Order blocked
phases.description: This response cannot overtake an older same-ID transaction when the AXI ordering rules require order.

phases.name: Eligible
phases.description: Only after the ordering dependency clears can the system QoS policy choose this request.

annotations.message: Arm recommends higher values as higher priority, but the protocol permits additional interpretations and does not mandate an instantaneous grant.
QoS selection applies only when no other AXI constraint already dictates transaction order.
